title: Letter 45 — My Counsel to a Young Priest
attribution_note: Letter 45 of 46 in the collection Letters Sent — see Letter 1 for provenance.

sections.heading: The fear of God and the priest's charge

pairs.en: My counsel.

I. Always strive to have the fear of God, and pray to God that He Himself may plant His fear in you. Fear is born, with God's help, from attention: who are you, and what is committed to you to keep? You are a priest and a pastor; keep, then, the sheep of Christ, which He purchased with His own Blood, and for them you shall give answer to Christ, how you kept them. Remember death, the Judgment of Christ, the heavenly kingdom and eternal torment; remember them always.

sections.heading: Guard purity of soul and body

pairs.en: II. You are young: keep the purity of soul and body. Look not intently upon the young faces of maidens and of women, lest Satan trouble your heart. Guard yourself from idle words, from jests, from laughter and from every kind of sport; think always that you walk before the face of God, and that God always looks upon you, and sees clearly your every deed, word and thought. Withdraw from dinners and from gatherings, that you may avoid sin. Where laughter, jests and talk of people are found, flee from that place.

Do not go to funeral feasts and other dinners; only, having performed the burial in the church, hasten home, for at those funeral dinners there is much that is a cause of stumbling. Take extreme care not to give offence, either by word or by deed: *“woe unto him, through whom they come,”* saith Christ [Luke 17:1]. What your fellow priests do, and what other people do, do not look at; but attend to what Christ teaches and commands. Often remember the sufferings of Christ: who He is, and how dreadful a torment He endured for us! Forget not the poor, but provide for them as you are able.

At the divine service, and especially at the Liturgy, strive earnestly to stand with compunction and with fear, remembering that you stand before the dread God and pray for yourself and for the people; and likewise perform the Holy Mysteries with great reverence.
Never be without work.
Pray often to God.

Read often the First Epistle of St John the Theologian: there the whole Christian duty is set forth; and also both Epistles to Timothy and the Epistle to Titus — there the duty of the servants of Christ is described. Read other books also; and whatever you read that is worthy, write it into notebooks, that you may be able, as occasion serves, to instruct the people.

sections.heading: Christian marriage, and the hearing of confessions

pairs.en: III. Live with your wife as a Christian, and not as the beasts do. At the time of the divine service, and before the service, withdraw from her: you know what I write here. Exhort her also, that she love purity. Read the First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 7, and especially the twenty-ninth verse.

IV. At confession proceed with great caution: take care that you bring not the sinner into despair; take care also that the sinner enter not into a habit of sin. Into habit the sinner comes easily, when sin goes without chastisement. Commonly the priests say, “God will forgive, God will forgive” — but look what his repentance is: whether he truly repents, and whether he promises henceforth to leave off from sin. Likewise a sinner may fall into despair when the priest deals harshly with him, sets forth the weight of the sin, and does not expound the great mercy of God. In such a case the priest must set before the unrepentant the righteous judgment of God, and before those who truly repent the unsearchable mercy of God. I cannot write all of this here; read the little book on confession given by your former bishop.
Beware of hearing the confessions of young women and of maidens, for you yourself are young, lest Satan sow tares in your heart. Let another priest confess them.

sections.heading: Teach the people, and rebuke without respect of persons

pairs.en: V. After the Liturgy always read something, though it be brief, for the instruction of the people; and leave no feast without instruction; and when you are somewhere in the parish, in anyone's house, speak something profitable to the soul, that the people may be built up in the spirit. If you know of any man that he sins in something, exhort him and entreat him that he leave off from sin, and terrify him with the Judgment of God, and with eternal torment, and with the unknown end of this life. Woe to Christians who are unamended, and to priests who do not strive to amend them!

Be ashamed of no man's face, and fear none, but rebuke all who sin; for this is the priestly calling; and ask of God help for all, though for this the wicked will hate you and speak evil of you. Fear them not; do your own work — God will defend you.

VI. Evil customs — as, for instance, swearing by God: “Yes, by God,” “God is my witness,” and other such calling upon the name of God in low matters — rebuke and root out, for in this men sin heavily. The same God who commands, *“Thou shalt have no other gods before Me”* [Exodus 20:3], commands also: *“Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain”* [Exodus 20:7]. Likewise when one condemns another, and when one says of another, “God judge him,” and the like — root out and rebuke all this evil.
VII. Remind all that the Judgment of Christ is *“at the doors”* [Matthew 24:33]; the day of Christ is already at hand; the Lord has prepared His throne for judgment. From this fear may be born.

VIII. The ten holy commandments read often yourself, with the interpretation, and read them also to your people. They are excellently interpreted in the little book of Plato, tutor of the Grand Duke; I think many in Voronezh have it.

IX. Do not please the rich, your friends, or persons of honour; for it is a great sin to please men. But what you see amiss in them, rebuke; and threaten those who are unamended with the fear of the Judgment of God.

sections.heading: Endure persecution with joy, and order your private life

pairs.en: X. So, if, walking in your duty, you are despised, and must endure evil speaking, slander and other persecutions from the lawless, make light of it — nay, rather rejoice, according to Christ's word: *“Rejoice, and be exceeding glad: for great is your reward in heaven”* [Matthew 5:12]. Amen.
Remember me also, a sinner.

Copy here the “Exhortation of the Venerable Moses” (it is written in the Prologue for the fifteenth day of December), and read it often, and attend to it, and strive to walk thus; and God the Merciful, seeing your zeal and diligence, will enlighten your mind by His grace and will help you — which I earnestly desire for you.

Living in your cell, walk thus. Rising from sleep, thank God and pray; coming from church, read something from books for the profit of your soul, then take up handiwork and do it. Having worked a while, rise and pray; having prayed, again read something from a book.

And so do all things in turn: that is, now pray, now read, now occupy yourself with handiwork. But in handiwork and in reading lift up your mind to Christ, and pray to Him that He have mercy upon you and help you.

If you do all things in turn, then for everything — for reading, for prayer — there will be the greater desire and zeal; for change gives desire and zeal. So men go from place to place and walk about; so also a change of food is more pleasant to men than one food always set before them. Change your work also, that you may come to it the more willingly.

If despondency, boredom and heaviness trouble you greatly, go out of your cell and walk where you may; and as you walk, sigh unto Christ, that He help you. Often remember death, the Judgment of Christ and eternity. By this remembrance, as by a scourge, all despondency, boredom and heaviness are driven away. All that is temporal is short and soon passes; but that which shall be after death abides for ever. The day passes, and with the day all things pass — that is, sorrow and joy — and so all life passes, and draws nearer and nearer to death. And in whatever state death finds a man, in that he shall appear in that age. Blessed is he who watches and awaits the hour of death!
Be saved in Christ, and remember me, the infirm, in your prayers.

*“Remember us, O Lord, in Thy kingdom”* — make this prayer often, with zeal, to Christ the Son of God, who sitteth on the right hand of God the Father in the glory of the Father. There sigh also for me, a sinner.
May the Lord Jesus Christ, our Saviour, have mercy upon us all, and make us worthy of the portion of His elect! Amen.

Postscript. Beware of going about as a guest, lest among men you scatter what you gather in solitude. It is rare that a man returns to his cell such as he was when he went out from his cell among the people. The desert and solitude gather good; but the scandals of the world scatter it.
Nowhere does a man repent better than in solitude. There a man gathers into his mind all his past life, and looking upon it, sighs unto Christ, and asks mercy of Him.

With nothing does a man sin so much as with the tongue; and in solitude he flees from this sin. Our eyes and ears are as doors, by which scandals come to the heart and strike upon it; and solitude flees from this, and will not even receive the scandal. Especially the young, and those who live without marriage, in whom the blood boils, ought to hold to solitude, that they may neither give nor receive scandal.

Attend well to this, and consider what I write. We read in history that pillars fell because of the flesh. What then may one expect of reeds? The desert and solitude, with God's help, preserve from this. A certain saint heard a voice: “Flee from men, that thou mayest be saved.” Let this voice sound also for us.

Yet in fleeing from men, we must flee not because of men, but because of sin. We must hate sin, and not men; and we must love them, and not hate them, but pray for them. To pray for ourselves is our necessity; to pray for our neighbours, love constrains us.
